deed: Amnon Shashua and his colleagues developed a wearable camera that reads text aloud to the blind and recognizes faces
title: Amnon Shashua and Ziv Aviram developed a camera for eyeglasses that reads text aloud to the blind and recognizes faces

trailer.text: In 2010, Prof. Amnon Shashua and Ziv Aviram, the founders of Mobileye, established OrCam, an Israeli company from Jerusalem.
When Shashua's aunt began to lose her sight, she asked him to find a solution.
A team of 120 developers worked on a single product, MyEye: a small camera on eyeglasses that reads text aloud, recognizes faces and announces the person's name.
According to The Jewish Chronicle, by 2017 several thousand devices had been sold in 12 countries.
Time magazine included the device in its list of the 100 best inventions of 2019.

paragraphs.text: Prof. Amnon Shashua specializes in computer vision.
He holds the Sachs Chair in computer science at the Hebrew University.
Together with Ziv Aviram, he had already founded Mobileye.
Intel acquired Mobileye in a $15.3 billion deal.
When Shashua's aunt began to lose her sight, she asked her nephew to find a solution.
Elad Sarfati of OrCam said that when they thought about who could use artificial vision, they thought about people who cannot see.
Dr. Yonatan Wexler also came to the field through his family: his sister lost sight in one eye and had blurry vision in the other, due to a tumor.
According to Wexler, one in every 2,000 people is totally blind, one in every 200 has impaired vision, and at age 60 the problem affects one in three.
In 2010, Shashua and Aviram founded OrCam.
According to a May 2017 article, Aviram served as CEO and Shashua as CTO, and these were also their roles at Mobileye at the time.
A team of 120 software, hardware and algorithm developers worked on a single product, which eventually became MyEye.
According to The Jewish Chronicle, Wexler developed MyEye with the Israeli founders over five years.
The engineers faced challenges: making the technology wearable, building a long-lasting battery, and keeping it easy to use.
OrCam has a long history of partnership with Intel, which invested in it.
In October 2013, OrCam began distributing its devices in limited quantities.
According to The Irish Times, the original MyEye launched in 2015, and according to the Jerusalem Report, in the same year the company expanded to more customers in the US.

stations.title: Point a finger, and the device reads

paragraphs.text: A TechCrunch team visited OrCam's offices in Jerusalem and found that using it is intuitive: you point your finger at what you want to read and wait a few seconds.
In December 2017, OrCam presented the second generation, MyEye 2.0.
The next generation is much smaller, because it works without the cumbersome companion device.
It is a finger-sized device with a camera and a microphone that clips onto eyeglasses and reads printed and digital text aloud.
Wexler explained that the device translates reading, a complex visual task, into hearing.
According to him, it reads text from any surface in real time.
In face recognition, the device detects that a person is in front of it and announces their name with a recording the user made in advance.
According to Wexler, the camera can store images of up to 100 faces and 150 objects.

At CES 2020, the device's spatial orientation capability, which guides the user to an object with beeps, relied on a library of 15 objects it can recognize, and Shashua said the library was expected to grow.
A Walla reporter said that in his test, the device recognized him by name, understood which banknote he was holding and read a passage from a digital newspaper.
In January 2020, OrCam unveiled new capabilities that allow the user to give the device voice commands.
Shashua said that with a phone bill, he does not want the device to read out everything, only the bottom line.
At CES 2020, the new functions were available only in English, and the company planned to add more languages by the end of that year.
The device works in several languages, and the sources give different numbers.
According to Shashua, the device does not require an internet connection or cloud computing.
According to Walla, all the data the camera captures is processed on the device itself and is not sent to the company's cloud.
Leon Paul of OrCam said the company kept the device self-sufficient, not relying on the internet, because of concern for the privacy of the visually impaired.
The images the device takes are not stored and are not sent.
The exception is biometric maps of faces the user asks it to learn, and these are stored on the device.
According to Wexler, the device does not store information about the documents the user "reads".
At a Jerusalem Post conference in New York, a radio host named Pedro took the stage and demonstrated how the device reads books aloud to him.
He said that in the past he waited until someone had time to read the mail for him.
Now, he said, he can read his mail in privacy, in his home.
According to Leon Paul, the device makes it possible once again to sit at home and read a book or a newspaper, sort mail, read a menu and stay at work.
There is also a version of the product for people with dyslexia.
According to the Jerusalem Report article, dyslexic children and students may, with the help of the camera, get the chance to excel in the classroom alongside their peers.

A 2016 JAMA Ophthalmology study among 12 legally blind participants showed that the device improved their ability to perform tasks simulating everyday activities, such as reading a message on an electronic device, a newspaper article or a menu.
OrCam is a Jerusalem company, and in July 2024 it announced that it would halt development of its flagship visual-aid product.
In 2024, after three rounds of layoffs, it was left with only several dozen employees.
According to The Jewish Chronicle, after the American launch and the opening of the offices in London and Toronto, several thousand devices were sold in 12 countries.
Ziv Aviram said the technology provides a solution for three large populations, which together number more than a billion people.
In Israel, OrCam cooperated with the Education Ministry and with Bituach Leumi (the National Insurance Institute) so that more people would gain access to the devices.
Full or partial funding can be obtained from bodies such as the Defense Ministry and Bituach Leumi.
In the US, according to Wexler, coverage was achieved with offices in individual states, such as the California Department of Rehabilitation.
Similar departments in about 10 US states, as well as the federal Department of Veterans Affairs, are beginning to provide OrCam's systems.
According to The Jerusalem Post, the MyEye cost $3,500, and the MyReader, which only reads, cost $2,500.
After a $41 million funding round, OrCam was valued at about $600 million.
In an interview with the Jerusalem Post in April, at a time when Mobileye was about to be sold to Intel, Wexler said the company was aiming for an IPO within about two years of that time.
The device was included in Time magazine's list of the 100 best inventions of 2019.
OrCam won the Last Gadget Standing award at the CES exhibition in Las Vegas.
Wexler said OrCam is revolutionizing the vision impaired community, just as hearing aids revolutionized the hearing impaired community 50 years ago.
The next device, OrCam Hear, is meant to solve "the cocktail party problem", which has occupied scientists for decades.
According to Calcalist, hearing aids amplify all voices indiscriminately, creating cacophony.
The small device hangs around the user's neck like a locket.
Shashua said the company has been working on combining video and acoustic waves for two years, and that the product will be released to the market by mid-2020.
According to Calcalist, the device was named Best of Innovation in the CES 2020 Innovation Awards.
Shashua also mentioned physicians.

According to Shashua, research shows that about 40% of physicians' time is spent in front of the computer. According to him, a device the company is working on, which would identify the participants in a conversation and the words of the doctor and the patient, could save up to 90% of the time spent writing reports.
TechCrunch noted that the device costs $3,500, an expensive price, but one that makes sense for a medical assistive device.
According to the Jerusalem Report article, expanding nationwide coverage in the US is more challenging, because of the private insurance framework.
OrCam briefly offered age estimation in face recognition, but dropped it because it was not reliable enough.
About OrCam Hear, Shashua said the device is still far from complete and voices are still transmitted with delays, but the hardware is working and only final tunings remain.
